case_study_insert.main_stem: Sunrise Palm Adventures (SPA) is a private limited company in the tourism and leisure sector, running an island resort with diving and water sports and employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 2010 by Diego Reyes, SPA has a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership, so dive masters and supervisors are consulted on operations. It plans to invest $640,000 in an overwater villa and a new dive centre, financed by a $360,000 ten-year bank loan and $280,000 retained profit. SPA has fixed costs of $195,000 a year, a variable cost of $22.00 a unit and a selling price of $37.00, and currently produces 20,000 units a year, each unit being one guest-night. Staff turnover has reached 16% and the dive-centre equipment defect rate is 5.2%, worrying Diego.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Resort Operations Report — Q3 2025: SPA hosted 5,100 guest-nights at $37.00 each, with 82% occupancy. The dive centre logged a 5.2% defect rate in equipment checks, up from 3.0% last year. Maintenance complaints rose from 21 to 39 per month. A survey of 550 resort guests found 70% rated the beach location as the top reason for booking and 62% would pay $2.00 more for certified dive equipment. A new dive kit costs $130.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Sunrise Palm Adventures as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Tourism Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.0% to 5.5%, increasing costs on SPA's $360,000 variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.0% from $12.50 to $13.38 per hour from April 2026, raising the resort wage bill. (3) Imported resort supplies and dive-equipment input costs have risen 10.8% year-on-year while tourism inflation is 6.6%, and island arrivals grew 3.9%.

questions.question_text: SPA is funding its new villa and dive centre partly with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for SPA of using retained profit instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The $280,000 of retained profit costs no interest or capital repayments, easing cash flow while SPA has fixed costs of $195,000 a year and a $360,000 loan to service. Money not paid as interest can replace the $130 dive kits needed to cut the 5.2% defect rate and tackle the 16% staff turnover, protecting the $15.00 contribution on each $37.00 guest-night.

Point 2: Retained profit needs no security, so the $640,000 villa and dive centre cannot be repossessed if the 82% occupancy falls. Diego Reyes and his managers also keep full control of the hierarchical structure and democratic decisions without a lender's conditions, which matters when 60 staff depend on the resort and maintenance complaints have risen to 39 a month. The 1.5-point rise to 5.5% would add roughly $5,400 a year on a variable-rate $360,000 loan, so using retained profit keeps that cash for the 60 staff and the dive centre. It also lets Diego Reyes fund the $130 dive kits needed to cut the 5.2% defect rate.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to SPA, its loan and its resort operations.

questions.question_text: SPA is promoting its new overwater villa and dive centre. Consider an international travel magazine, regional television, or social media influencer marketing. Which should SPA choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
International travel magazine: A glossy magazine advert can showcase the overwater villa to a wealthy, travel-minded audience and build a premium image for the $640,000 investment. However, rates are high and lead times long, and print cannot show the dive experience dynamically or take immediate bookings, so conversion of the 550 surveyed guests may be slow.

Regional television: TV can reach a large audience quickly with film of the villa and water sports, raising awareness across the region. Yet airtime is expensive for a company with 60 staff and a $360,000 loan, and many viewers live too far to book a $37.00 guest-night, so much of the spend would be wasted.

Social media influencer marketing: Travel and diving influencers can demonstrate the new dive centre and villa directly to exactly the 70% of guests drawn by the beach location and the 62% who would pay $2.00 more for certified equipment. Engagement is measurable and cost per lead low, though results take time and depend on credible creators.

Recommendation: SPA should choose social media influencer marketing. It targets the segments in the 550-guest survey, is far cheaper than regional television and more immediate and visual than print, while showing off the $640,000 villa and dive centre. Magazines are rejected as slow and passive; television is rejected as costly and geographically wasteful. A small magazine feature could support the campaign later. With maintenance complaints up to 39 a month, the promoted image must match what guests experience at the 82% occupancy resort. Influencer content can showcase the new villa honestly, while the 70% who value the beach location and 62% who want certified equipment are reached directly.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of SPA with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of SPA with a well-justified recommendation explaining why magazines and television are rejected.

questions.question_text: Staff turnover at SPA has reached 16%. Explain two benefits for SPA of using financial motivators such as bonuses to improve staff retention.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Bonuses tied to service targets give SPA's 60 staff a direct financial reason to stay and improve the resort, helping cut the 16% turnover and the cost of repeatedly replacing $130 dive kits and retraining. Higher retention protects the 82% occupancy and the $37.00 guest-night price, while experienced staff keep the 5.2% equipment defect rate under control.

Point 2: Performance-related pay can raise effort and quality, tackling the rise in maintenance complaints from 21 to 39 a month because staff gain when guests are satisfied. With democratic leadership and dive masters consulted, a fair bonus scheme reinforces their contribution, supports the 62% of guests who would pay more for certified dive equipment and steadies the workforce during the $640,000 villa and dive-centre project. Retaining experienced staff also protects the 5,100 guest-nights sold last quarter and reduces the risk that the 5.2% defect rate rises again. A stable team can keep the 21-to-39 complaint trend from worsening, which matters while SPA invests $640,000 in the villa and dive centre.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SPA's turnover, complaints and service quality.

questions.question_text: SPA must reduce its 5.2% defect rate in dive-centre equipment checks. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local marine college. Which should SPA choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching staff on SPA's own dive kits and checking routines is directly relevant, costs no fees and keeps the 60 staff productive while they learn, protecting the 5,100 guest-nights sold last quarter and the drive to cut the 5.2% defect rate. The drawback is that senior dive masters acting as trainers have less time for guests, bad habits may spread, and there is no external certificate for the 62% of guests who value certified equipment.

Off-the-job training: The local marine college offers structured checking procedures and a recognised qualification, which supports the 62% of surveyed guests who would pay $2.00 more for certified dive equipment. However, it takes staff away from the resort, cutting capacity at 82% occupancy, and the generic course may not match SPA's exact kits, so on-site follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: SPA should choose on-the-job training first, with short college certification for senior dive masters. It is cheaper, kit-specific and avoids losing resort capacity while the defect rate is 5.2% and turnover 16%. Full off-the-job training is rejected because withdrawing many staff would disrupt guest service and add fees on top of a $640,000 investment; college modules can follow once standards are stable. Senior dive masters can coach on the real $130 kits, which is more useful than a generic course when 62% of guests value certified equipment. Keeping the 60 staff on site also protects 82% occupancy, whereas sending several divers away would strain service during the $640,000 expansion. The marine college can still certify senior divers once the villa launch is complete and capacity recovers.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to SPA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of SPA.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of SPA with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and safety relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how SPA's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $195,000 ÷ ($37.00 − $22.00) = $195,000 ÷ $15.00 = 13,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 13,000 guest-night units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $37.00 − $22.00 = $15.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $15.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways SPA's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Managers can compare the 13,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 20,000 guest-nights to confirm the resort is profitable, leaving a margin of safety of 7,000 guest-nights.
2. Contribution per unit of $15.00 lets SPA model the $2.00 premium that 62% of guests would pay for certified dive equipment, showing how the $640,000 villa and dive centre could be recovered.
3. The break-even figure helps plan interest on the $360,000 loan and check whether 20,000 guest-nights generate enough contribution to cover fixed costs of $195,000 before more borrowing.
4. Average total cost of $31.75 a unit ($195,000 ÷ 20,000 + $22.00) can be benchmarked against 82% occupancy, the 5.2% defect rate and 16% turnover, guiding the $130 dive-kit spend as input costs rise 10.8%.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 13,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $15.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 20,000 guest-nights; modelling the $2.00 certified-equipment premium; loan planning for the $640,000 investment; and average total cost benchmarking at $31.75 to tackle defects and turnover.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SPA's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has SPA's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.58 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.35 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.08 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.88 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $65,000 inventories + $95,000 trade receivables + $45,000 cash = $205,000; 2025 current assets = $80,000 + $120,000 + $30,000 = $230,000. Dividing by current liabilities gives 2024 = $205,000 ÷ $130,000 = 1.58 and 2025 = $230,000 ÷ $170,000 = 1.35. Excluding inventories, 2024 = ($205,000 − $65,000) ÷ $130,000 = 1.08 and 2025 = ($230,000 − $80,000) ÷ $170,000 = 0.88.

Evaluation: Liquidity has weakened. The 2024 figure of 1.58 fell to 1.35 because current liabilities jumped from $130,000 to $170,000 while cash fell from $45,000 to $30,000. The stricter measure, which removes inventories, dropped from 1.08 to 0.88, so SPA now depends on selling its growing $80,000 of stock to meet short-term debts — risky while it services a $360,000 loan and spends $640,000 on the villa. Trade receivables also rose from $95,000 to $120,000, tying up cash.

Conclusion: SPA's financial position has not improved; it has deteriorated. Both measures fell (1.58 to 1.35 and 1.08 to 0.88), driven by higher liabilities and lower cash. SPA should pause extra borrowing, collect the $120,000 of receivables and rebuild cash before committing fully to the $640,000 expansion. The higher $170,000 of liabilities leave little headroom for the 10.8% input inflation, so rebuilding cash matters before the $640,000 villa is finished. Collecting the $120,000 of receivables would ease the strain on both measures and restore a safer 1.35-plus position.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether SPA's position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SPA of introducing eco-friendly resort practices.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Protecting the marine environment supports the 70% of surveyed guests who book for the beach location and the 62% who would pay $2.00 more for certified dive equipment, reinforcing the $37.00 price. It also helps contain the $22.00 variable cost per guest-night as imported supplies rise 10.8%, strengthening the case for the $640,000 dive centre.

Disadvantage: Green measures such as reef conservation and waste systems add to fixed costs of $195,000 a year when SPA already has a $360,000 loan and has spent $640,000 on the villa. If 82% occupancy slips, these costs are harder to recover, and any disruption could worsen the 5.2% equipment defect rate and the 39 monthly maintenance complaints. If the 62% premium is not won, the green spending simply adds to fixed costs of $195,000 without lifting the $37.00 price. Protecting the marine setting that draws 70% of guests is therefore both an ethical and a commercial necessity for SPA.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SPA's survey, costs and resort operations.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.5%, the 7.0% minimum wage increase and the 10.8% rise in imported supplies and dive-equipment costs will affect SPA. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.0% to 5.5%): If SPA's $360,000 ten-year loan is variable-rate, annual interest rises by 1.5% of $360,000 = $5,400. That is modest beside fixed costs of $195,000, and if the loan is fixed the direct cost is nil. Higher rates may still cool island tourism, but SPA can cap the risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage increase (7.0%, to $13.38 per hour): With a workforce of 60, many resort and dive roles are hourly-paid, so the rise feeds into the wage bill. The insert states no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual total can be invented; the honest comparison is the given output of 20,000 guest-nights across 60 staff, about 333 guest-nights per worker. If productivity holds and 16% turnover falls, the $15.00 contribution can absorb it; otherwise unit labour cost rises.

Imported supplies and dive-equipment inflation (10.8%): The $22.00 variable cost per unit is where these costs sit, but the insert gives no breakdown, so only a bound is defensible: if the whole $22.00 rose 10.8%, that is 0.108 × $22.00 = $2.38 per unit, about $47,520 a year at 20,000 guest-nights. Even a $2.00-per-unit rise costs $40,000 a year, cutting contribution from $15.00 toward $13.00.

Conclusion: The 10.8% rise in imported supplies and dive-equipment costs will have the greatest impact because it recurs on all 20,000 guest-nights and directly erodes the $15.00 contribution supporting the $640,000 investment. The wage rise is meaningful but manageable if productivity holds, while the interest rise adds only about $5,400.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to SPA.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on SPA's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of SPA with a well-justified judgment that imported input inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
